opus-5.5.text:
I think the way to think about those tasks is not so much that folding laundry or assembling a box is the end goal in itself, but that they're really good stress tests for the kind of physical intelligence we actually care about. Laundry is a great example because it's deformable, every shirt starts in a different crumpled configuration, there's no simple script you can write for it. If you want to get it right, the robot has to perceive the state of the cloth, recover from mistakes, regrasp when something slips, and do all of that over a fairly long horizon. That's a lot of the ingredients of general-purpose manipulation packed into one task that's easy for a person to evaluate.

Now, the role of the demonstrations specifically is that they give us a way to get competent behavior into the model in the first place. We collect teleoperated data across many robots and many tasks, and the model learns from all of it together. What we've found is that the dexterous, hard tasks actually help the general model, not just themselves. When you train on a lot of diverse, difficult manipulation data, the model picks up representations of how objects move, how contacts work, how to correct errors, and that transfers. So the box folding data isn't only teaching box folding; it's teaching something about careful bimanual manipulation that shows up elsewhere.

But I'd also be honest that demonstrations alone aren't the full story. Imitation gets you to a point where the robot can do the task reasonably well, but to get really robust and really fast, you need the robot to improve from its own experience, with reinforcement learning, with feedback, with practice. Demonstrations are kind of like the pretraining phase. They give you a prior that's good enough that the robot is making meaningful attempts, and then autonomous improvement is what takes it the rest of the way.

And the bigger picture, the reason I'm excited about this, is that it mirrors what happened with language models. You train a big foundation model on broad data, and then you can adapt it to lots of downstream things. If we can get robots to the point where the base model already has a lot of physical common sense from these diverse dexterous tasks, then teaching it a new task becomes much cheaper. That's really the path to general-purpose robots: not hand-engineering each skill, but building up a foundation that makes each new skill easy.

r001.rationale: The response describes dexterous tasks as stress tests for physical intelligence and demonstrations as training data that helps models learn and transfer skills. It does not identify validating the soundness of the underlying robotics methods as their purpose.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think people sometimes look at those demos, the laundry folding, the box assembly, and they read them as the point. Like the goal is a robot that folds laundry. And that's not really how I think about it. The reason we picked those tasks is that they're hard in a very specific way. They're long horizon, they involve deformable objects, there's a huge amount of variability in the initial state, and you can't really hand-engineer your way through them. If a shirt comes out of the dryer in a crumpled ball, there's no clean geometric description of that. So they're a good stress test for whether the thing you built actually has a general capability or whether it's just a well-tuned pipeline for one setup.

The analogy I'd draw is to language models. Nobody trained GPT-style models because they cared about predicting the next token. Next-token prediction was the thing that forced the model to acquire a lot of general structure about the world. For robots, I think dexterous manipulation plays a similar role. If you can get a model to handle laundry robustly, it has to have some understanding of contact, of how objects respond to forces, of what to do when something goes wrong partway through. Those are exactly the things you need for basically everything else.

Now, there's a distinction I'd make between the demonstration as a product and the demonstration as a signal. As a product, a laundry-folding robot is fine, there's probably a business there. But what we actually care about is the scaling question. Does performance on these tasks keep improving as you add more data, more diverse data, data from other embodiments, data from the web? If the answer is yes, then you have something that behaves like a foundation model, and the specific task is kind of incidental. If the answer is no, if you saturate and you need a bespoke solution for each task, then you're back in the old paradigm and the demo doesn't mean very much.

And I'd say the honest state of things is that we're seeing the former, but it's early. The pretraining data matters a lot. Having a broad base of manipulation experience across many tasks and many robots, and then fine-tuning on something like box folding, works much better than training on box folding from scratch. That's the result that makes me optimistic. It means the dexterous demos aren't a dead end, they're a readout of how much general knowledge the model has accumulated.

The other thing I'd say is that these tasks force you to confront the parts of the problem that are easy to ignore. Grasping a mug on a table is a bit of a trap, because you can get very far with tricks. When the task is thirty seconds of continuous contact-rich manipulation, every small error compounds, and the model has to recover from its own mistakes. Learning that recovery behavior is, I think, most of what separates something that works in a lab from something that works in a home. So I'd put it this way: the demos aren't the destination, they're the instrument we're using to find out whether we're on the right road.

r001.rationale: The response describes dexterous tasks as stress tests for whether the system has genuine general capability rather than a task-specific pipeline, and calls the demos an instrument for judging whether the approach is on the right road.

astra-6.text:
I think the important question is what those demonstrations tell us about generalization. Folding a shirt is a very difficult manipulation problem: the object changes shape, you have to infer things you can’t directly see, and you have to continually adjust what you’re doing. So it’s a useful task to study. But a robot that folds one particular shirt in one particular setup isn’t necessarily making progress toward being general purpose.

What would be much more compelling is if training on folding laundry also made the robot better at something else—packing a bag, for example—or if experience with many other tasks let it learn to fold laundry with very little additional data. Then you’re seeing evidence of reusable knowledge, rather than just a solution to one task.

Demonstrations are a good way to get that process started. They show the robot what successful behavior looks like without requiring it to discover everything through trial and error. But I think you also want the robot to learn from its own experience. If it makes a mistake halfway through folding something, it needs to recover from the situation it actually created, which might be quite different from anything in the demonstrations.

So I’d view these tasks as both sources of training experience and tests of a broader system. The goal isn’t really to collect an impressive list of chores. It’s to build a learning process where each new chore makes the next one easier.

r001.rationale: The response says dexterous tasks can test whether a broader system learns reusable knowledge and generalizes, but it does not identify validating the soundness of the underlying robotics methods as their purpose.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important question is what the robot has to learn to do those tasks, rather than whether folding a particular box is itself useful. Laundry is a good example because the object doesn’t have a fixed shape. You have to perceive what state it’s in, take an action, see what happened, and adjust. It’s difficult to solve that with a fixed sequence of motions.

But a demonstration of that behavior doesn’t, by itself, establish generality. You’d want to know: Can it handle a shirt it hasn’t seen before? What happens if the shirt starts in a different configuration? If it makes a mistake, can it recover? Those variations are where you start to distinguish a system that has learned something reusable from one that has learned a narrow routine.

So I would view these tasks as useful ingredients in a much broader training process. The exciting possibility is that learning many different manipulation tasks gives you shared capabilities—understanding contact, tracking objects, correcting errors—that make the next task easier to learn. That transfer is ultimately what we need for a general-purpose robot.

r001.rationale: The response frames demonstrations as a way to build and assess reusable capabilities and transfer, but does not identify validating the soundness of the underlying robotics methods as their purpose.
